meta.title: Who really said "I am a firm believer in the people. If given the truth, they can be depended upon to meet any national crisis. The great point is to bring them the real facts"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Douglas MacArthur wrote it in a 1944 letter to Rep. A. L. Miller, opening "Like Abraham Lincoln." Later trimmed and misattributed to Lincoln himself.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I am a firm believer in the people. If given the truth, they can be depended upon to meet any national crisis. The great point is to bring them the real facts'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Lincoln. Douglas MacArthur wrote it in a 1944 letter to Rep. A. L. Miller, beginning "Like Abraham Lincoln." The popular version trims that opening.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From MacArthur’s February 1944 letter to Rep. A. L. Miller of Nebraska, made public in April 1944. The circulating version is a light trim: the original begins “Like Abraham Lincoln,” and reads “any national crises” and “bring before them the real facts.”

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: Letter to Rep. A. L. Miller (R–Nebraska)
February 1944, replying to Miller’s letter of January 27
April 1944, released to the press by Miller without MacArthur’s consent
John Gunther, The Riddle of MacArthur (London: Hamish Hamilton, 1951), p. 54

source.excerpt:
I appreciate very much your scholarly letter of Jan. 27. Your description of conditions in the United States is a sobering one indeed and is calculated to arouse the thoughtful consideration of every true patriot.

We must not inadvertently slip into the same condition internally as the one which we fight externally. Like Abraham Lincoln, I am a firm believer in the people, and, if given the truth, they can be depended upon to meet any national crises. The great point is to bring before them the real facts.
trail: Barry Popik transcribes the letter from the Tuscaloosa News, 14 April 1944, and from Time, 24 April 1944. Both versions include “Like Abraham Lincoln”: Popik, “I am a firm believer in the people” ↗
Wikiquote’s sourced MacArthur section lists the line from the Tuscaloosa News of April 14, 1944: Wikiquote: Douglas MacArthur ↗
John Gunther reprints the full exchange of letters with Miller and dates this reply to February 1944: Gunther, The Riddle of MacArthur (1951), pp. 53–54 ↗
Wikiquote lists the trimmed version as misattributed to Lincoln “by several authors since about 2000”: Wikiquote: Abraham Lincoln, Misattributed ↗
source.excerptNote: Text as printed in Gunther (1951), p. 54, and as transcribed by Barry Popik from the Tuscaloosa News of 14 April 1944. The popular quotation drops “Like Abraham Lincoln,” and changes “crises” to “crisis” and “bring before them” to “bring them.”

author.name: Douglas MacArthur
author.heading: About Douglas MacArthur
author.bio: Douglas MacArthur was Chief of Staff of the U.S. Army in the 1930s and Supreme Commander, Southwest Pacific Area, in the Second World War. He later oversaw the occupation of Japan and led the United Nations Command in Korea. In 1944, while still commanding in the Pacific, he was the reluctant focus of a Republican presidential boomlet, and this letter came out of that episode.

copyAttribution: "I am a firm believer in the people. If given the truth, they can be depended upon to meet any national crisis. The great point is to bring them the real facts." — Douglas MacArthur, letter to Rep. A. L. Miller, February 1944 (made public April 1944). Popular trimmed form; the original begins "Like Abraham Lincoln, I am a firm believer in the people…" and reads "crises" and "bring before them the real facts."

misattribution.heading: Why people credit Lincoln
misattribution.intro: The line is usually shared as a quotation from Abraham Lincoln. That comes from MacArthur’s own words. He began the sentence “Like Abraham Lincoln, I am a firm believer in the people,” and once that opening clause was cut, the comparison turned into an attribution.

items.why: No Lincoln source contains this wording. Wikiquote lists it under Lincoln’s misattributed quotes and traces it to MacArthur: Wikiquote ↗. Barry Popik also concludes that Lincoln “never said those exact words”: Popik ↗.

Some versions add a joke ending, “and beer.” Wikiquote says that phrase first appeared in an online list of jokes in 1999: Wikiquote ↗. Popik dates the ending in print to about 2005 and cites the Great Falls Tribune of 7 February 2005: Popik ↗.

A related Lincoln remark does exist: “I have faith in the people… Let them know the truth and the country is safe.” A Boston Journal correspondent reported it, and the Sandusky Register reprinted it on 29 April 1865: Popik ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Douglas MacArthur’s, from his 1944 letter to Rep. A. L. Miller, in which he compared himself to Lincoln: Popik’s transcription of the 1944 newspapers ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: In 1943 and 1944, Rep. A. L. Miller, a Nebraska congressman who opposed the New Deal, wrote to MacArthur urging him to let supporters draft him for president. MacArthur sent two replies. In April 1944 Miller gave them to the press without MacArthur’s knowledge or consent, even though one was marked ‘Personal’ (Gunther ↗).

Gunther writes that the letters “created a turbulent, brief storm.” Critics read MacArthur’s praise of Miller as an implied criticism of his commander-in-chief. MacArthur answered that the letters “were neither politically inspired nor intended to convey blanket approval of the Congressman’s views.” The line that now circulates as a tribute to democratic trust started as part of a political embarrassment.

sourcesVerified.claim: MacArthur's letter to Rep. A. L. Miller, printed in the Tuscaloosa News of 14 April 1944 and in Time of 24 April 1944, contains 'Like Abraham Lincoln, I am a firm believer in the people, and, if given the truth, they can be depended upon to meet any national crises. The great point is to bring before them the real facts.' It replied to Miller's letter of Jan 27. Lincoln never said the exact words, and the 'and beer' ending dates from about 2005 (Great Falls Tribune, 7 Feb 2005).

Gunther, The Riddle of MacArthur (Hamish Hamilton, 1951), pp. 53-54, reprints the Miller letters. Miller published them without consent and one was marked 'Personal'. The reply to Miller's Jan. 27 letter is dated February 1944 and contains the passage with 'Like Abraham Lincoln', 'crises' and 'bring before them the real facts'. Gunther says the letters 'created a turbulent, brief storm' and quotes MacArthur that they 'were neither politically inspired nor intended to convey blanket approval'.

Wikiquote lists the line under Lincoln's misattributed quotes: 'Misattributed to Lincoln by several authors since about 2000', with the source being MacArthur. It says 'and beer' first appeared in an online joke list in 1999.
Wikiquote's MacArthur page has the line in its sourced 1940s section, citing the Tuscaloosa News of April 14, 1944.

Lincoln's genuine remark 'I have faith in the people... Let them know the truth and the country is safe' was reported by a Boston Journal correspondent and reprinted in the Sandusky Register, 29 April 1865.
Douglas MacArthur was a U.S. General of the Army: Army Chief of Staff 1930-35, Supreme Commander Southwest Pacific Area in WWII, head of the occupation of Japan, and UN commander in Korea.
